title: Carrington clarifies 'white privilege' post after ejection backlash
dek: DiJonai Carrington was ejected from a Chicago Sky game after a hard foul on Sophie Cunningham drew criticism and a controversial social-media post. Carrington later clarified she never claimed the foul assessment itself was based on white privilege, and called on critics to research her educational background.
author: The GoCheckMySports Desk
key_fact: Carrington, who holds bachelor's degrees in psychology and African and African American Studies from Stanford, stated she never claimed the foul assessment was based on white privilege, but her original post's meaning remains disputed by commentators.
bottom_line: Carrington's clarification shifts the dispute from whether her post accused the official of racial bias to whether her original social-media statement was communicated clearly enough to avoid misinterpretation. The sources do not specify what her intended meaning was, leaving open what she meant to convey with the post.
body: DiJonai Carrington was ejected from the Chicago Sky's game against Indiana Fever after committing a hard foul on Sophie Cunningham. The foul was assessed as a Flagrant 2, per reporting from BBC Sport and Awful Announcing.
Carrington stated after the game that the foul was not intentional. However, she posted 'WHITE PRIVILEGE @indianafever' on social media following her ejection, according to Awful Announcing.

Sports commentator Emmanuel Acho responded sharply on his Speakeasy podcast, saying on BBC Sport: "It was not a race-based decision. To call that a white privilege-based foul is to completely undermine the term of white privilege and to also completely ignore the rules in basketball. You hit her in the head. You drew blood. You didn't connect with the ball at all whatsoever. So to me, it was just very ignorant and, to some degree, asinine by DiJonai Carrington to suggest that that call was based on white privilege."

Carrington responded on social media, per BBC Sport, stating: "I've never once claimed that the assessment of the foul was white privilege (that was your assumption). Try exercising your critical thinking skills, I know you studied psych. Furthermore, I'm the last thing from ignorant or asinine when it comes to speaking on 'white privilege', do ya research on that one. I actually went to school, one of the top universities might I add, to educate myself on this exact subject. I would never use that term as a rhetorical weapon knowing the historical and social weight it holds without having the proper evidence to substantiate it." According to Awful Announcing, Carrington holds bachelor's degrees from Stanford in both Psychology and African and African American Studies.

Acho, who holds a bachelor's degree in sports management and a master's degree in sports psychology from the University of Texas per Awful Announcing, acknowledged the pushback. According to Awful Announcing, he wrote "I stand corrected," but added that Carrington's message lacked clarity: "America is a speaker oriented country, so the burden is on you for being clear, direct and easy to understand." He elaborated further, saying per Awful Announcing: "Respectfully, the problem with Dijonai's tweet is nothing about it was clear. If we're ignoring the obvious context of her ejection, 'White privilege' becomes an explosive accusation with no context. White privilege is a real thing, it's not a claim you can ambiguously make."

Sophie Cunningham, the player fouled, said after her team's 90-86 victory over Chicago according to BBC Sport: "I think the league is taking care of that. This has nothing to do with race. Last year, I did the same thing and I got kicked out, and I deserved to be kicked out. There's no reason even to play that card."
